anchor_line: Our school notice board: which claims go beyond the evidence?

slides.title: Your first idea and reason
slides.text: Wet paper, an empty cup and frame droplets. What might explain them?
slides.caption: Record your confidence as well as your reason.

slides.title: BEFORE · keep our reasons
items: Share a prediction and its reason.
Keep a different idea visible.
slides.do: Invite two contrasting predictions from learners who have written individually. Record exact reasons without correction.

slides.title: GS12 · classify the six statements
rows: The paper beside the closed window is wet.
Rain must have entered through a gap.
A cup on the sill is empty.
Where did the water come from?
The window frame has droplets on it.
slides.caption: Reported observation, inference or question? Record alone.

slides.title: Compare possible explanations
items: Compare your six classifications.
Construct two explanations fitting two observations.
Keep the evidence for each separate.

slides.title: Which observation would help next?
items: Share one safe additional observation.
Explain how it could distinguish your two ideas.

slides.title: Which words report the evidence?
slides.caption: An inference interprets observations; it is not certain knowledge of an unseen cause.

slides.title: Does an empty cup prove a spill?
columns:
Rain entering
A spill
Another justified explanation
An empty cup alone does not identify the cause.
slides.caption: Condensation is another candidate if justified; avoid accusations.

slides.title: Write a limited explanation
items: Name one observation and two interpretations.
State a limit and a safe follow-up check.

slides.title: Our Driving Question Board
items: What would distinguish rain from a spill?
Separate a measurement from a witness report.
Keep untested explanations open.

slides.title: Revise your own model
items: Keep observation and inference in separate boxes.
Retain your first explanation; annotate changed confidence.

slides.title: Individual exit
items: Give one observation and two inferences.
Add one useful, safe additional check.

goals: State a conclusion within the test’s limits.

slides.title: Your first idea and reason
slides.text: Which paper would show greater water rise in 60 seconds? What must we measure?

slides.title: BEFORE · keep our reasons
items: Share a prediction and its reason.

slides.title: GS13 · printed illustrative readings
slides.caption: Printed illustrative fallback · equal 60 s tests · not your own measurements.

slides.title: Calculate each mean
items: Add the three rises for each paper.
Divide each total by the number of trials.
Keep millimetres in your record.

slides.title: Compare the pattern
items: Which mean is greater?
What varied between repeat readings?
What can this test actually support?

slides.title: Mean rise in this printed trial
slides.caption: B: (9 + 10 + 11)/3 = 10 mm

slides.title: Compare means without losing the conditions
slides.caption: Printed illustrative data · after equal 60 s tests.

slides.title: What can we infer?
items: Use “in these conditions” in your conclusion.
Name what was kept comparable.
State one untested property or limitation.

slides.title: Our Driving Question Board
items: Post today’s evidence.
Keep a question that needs more evidence.
Sort: answered, partly answered, still open.

slides.title: Revise your own model
items: Add collection, organisation and analysis to your evidence model.
Cite the labelled printed data; retain untested properties.

slides.title: Individual exit
items: Give a numerical conclusion with units.
State one limit of that conclusion.

3.route: Use the source-permitted printed illustrative fallback. This draft does not claim hands-on measurement. The optional real trial requires teacher preparation/access review; follow the unchanged source procedure and safety notes if selected.
3.preparation: One labelled GS13 data sheet per learner; notebook, pencil, ruler for the printed table and timer. The printed route requires no water or apparatus. Show or describe the two paper samples before prediction, without hinting at the result. If descriptions are unavailable, retain that uncertainty rather than invent paper properties.
3.decisions: Printed fallback chosen explicitly. Never present means or printed values as class observations. Source clean-water/paper trial remains an optional teacher-reviewed route, not a fabricated practical.

goals: Use counts to describe a change.

slides.title: Your first idea and reason
slides.text: The trays received different water amounts. Does that alone establish the cause?
slides.caption: Does water alone explain the difference? Give your first reason.

slides.title: BEFORE · keep our reasons
items: Share a prediction and its reason.
Keep a different idea visible.
slides.do: Invite two contrasting predictions from learners who have written individually. Record exact reasons without correction.

slides.title: GS14 · illustrative garden records
slides.caption: Illustrative records · not a real class experiment.

slides.title: Write a fairer comparison plan
items: Use all six GS14 plan headings.
Name the changed factor and comparable conditions.
Specify an outcome, repeats and a limitation.

slides.title: Ask a partner to test the plan
items: What else could explain the difference?
Does your plan separate those possibilities?

slides.title: Two differences changed together
columns:
P: 20 mL daily
Q: 40 mL daily

P: sunny room
Q: cooler shaded room
slides.caption: Light, temperature and location can confound the water claim.

slides.title: Defend a bounded conclusion
items: Say what the counts show.
Explain why water alone is not isolated.
Describe one concrete design improvement.

slides.title: Our Driving Question Board
items: Post today’s evidence.
Keep a question that needs more evidence.
Sort: answered, partly answered, still open.

slides.title: Revise your own model
items: Add competing explanations and fair comparison to your model.
Preserve the initial claim and revise with today’s record.

slides.title: Individual exit
items: Name one confound.
Give one concrete design change.

4.route: Written planning from illustrative GS14 records only; no seed-growing practical is added.

goals: Link each direction to source evidence.
Explain an interest and a next learning action.

slides.title: Your first idea and reason
slides.text: Which science-related career direction interests you? What would you like to know?

slides.title: BEFORE · a question about science work
items: Share a question about the work if you wish.
Keep a personal career choice private if you prefer.
slides.do: Invite voluntary questions about the work, not compulsory personal aspirations. Do not rank careers. Keep every learner’s private written reason.

slides.title: GS15 · two printed source summaries
columns: Weather/climate observations, analysis, forecasting and early warnings.
A national research role concerning human health.
slides.caption: Source-supplied paraphrases checked 13 November 2026; not quotations or qualification advice.

slides.title: Build your own career chart
items: Cover both directions using all GS15 columns.
Label suggested questions and evidence as examples.
Keep stated roles separate from your inferences.

slides.title: Check the source support
items: Verify statements against the printed summaries.
Use the optional approved official-page route only if provided.
Record actual navigation as observed or not observed.

slides.title: What do the source roles support?
columns:
Training requirements
Specific job duties
Qualifications or employment
slides.caption: A reasonable career inference is not a job guarantee.

slides.title: Connect evidence and possible benefit
items: Use source A or B for each career link.
Explain a possible community benefit as an example.

slides.title: Explain an interest without an overclaim
items: Give a reason for your chosen direction.
Name a training question that remains unverified.
Keep the two source limits visible.

slides.title: Our Driving Question Board
items: Post today’s evidence.
Keep a question that needs more evidence.
Sort: answered, partly answered, still open.

slides.title: Revise your own model
items: Add careers to your evidence model.
Write one attainable personal learning action and a reason.

slides.title: Individual exit
items: Submit your individual chart.
Explain why your next learning action matters.

5.route: Printed summaries remain the offline route. Optional official-page navigation uses only teacher-approved pages/cached copies. Print work is not evidence of digital navigation; no personal data or unrelated links.
5.preparation: GS15 printed source summaries and blank chart per learner. Optional supervised device access only if locally provided and observed.

goals: Connect scientific evidence with a possible use.
Revise a sourced message with limits.

slides.title: Your first idea and reason
slides.text: Which claim from our earlier work most needs a qualification?

slides.title: BEFORE · keep our reasons
items: Share a prediction and its reason.
Keep a different idea visible.
slides.do: Invite two contrasting predictions from learners who have written individually. Record exact reasons without correction.

slides.title: GS16 · draft the one-page message
items: Include life, environment and technology examples.
Explain each evidence-to-decision link.
Add a small career chart and a next learning action.

slides.title: Exchange one evidence-based critique
items: Identify one supported claim.
Identify one overclaim and ask a question.

slides.title: Choose a revision
items: Select a change your evidence supports.
Keep the first wording visible.

slides.title: From evidence to a possible use
slides.caption: Use a specific GS11–GS15 example; do not turn a proposed use into a tested outcome.

slides.title: Which claim respects the absorption test?
columns: Paper A had greater mean rise in the stated printed trial.
“Paper A is always best for every job.”
slides.caption: Material selection needs a test of the property required for that job.

slides.title: Explain why your revision is stronger
items: Cite the evidence and its source.
State the limit or uncertainty.
Explain the possible usefulness without promising an outcome.

slides.title: Our Driving Question Board
items: Post today’s evidence.
Keep a question that needs more evidence.
Sort: answered, partly answered, still open.

slides.title: Revise your own model
items: Revise the same message in a new colour.
Record a personal next action and retain a still-open question.

slides.title: Individual exit
items: Define General Science in your own words.
Give one useful link and one remaining uncertainty.

6.preparation: GS16 and earlier GS11–GS15 cards, learners’ own records, two colours and paper. No new practical or treatment/weather advice.

goals: Evaluate a claim and its limits.

slides.title: Independent work · procedure
items: Use only today’s data and assessment prompts.
Keep your working and reasons visible.
Work alone; submit before any discussion.

slides.title: Assessment · sections 1–2
items: Use only GS17 and the separate assessment prompts.
Show your own means, units and reasoning.
Keep observations and interpretations distinct.

slides.title: Assessment · sections 3–4
items: Complete the career/source and reflection prompts.
Check that evidence and limits are labelled.
Work independently; no exemplar is shown.

slides.title: A separate still-open scientific question
items: Write one still-open scientific question.
Explain what additional evidence could help.
Keep the question private until collection.

slides.title: Check and submit
items: Check names, units and completion.
Submit all sheets before any discussion.

7.preparation: Print only GS17 and the original independent assessment prompts. Basic calculator optional. Keep all teaching cards and exemplars private.
7.route: Independent printed assessment. Phase names are scheduling labels; no peer discussion, hints or answer correction before collection.
